headline: Biddeford Pool's Incoming Turns On: Bass to 30, Blues Chewing Through the Mackerel
subhead: The Harvest Moon tides are stacking bait against the rocks from Wells to Prouts Neck, and the stripers know it.
body_markdown:
The mate at the Pool ramp had a story worth repeating this week — a school of mackerel got pinned against the back side of the Pool on a hard incoming tide, and for about forty minutes the water inside the channel looked like it was boiling. Bass came up under them, blues came up under the bass, and every rod on the dock that morning had a story to tell by nine a.m. That's the pattern right now up and down this stretch, and it's only going to get more consistent as the Harvest Moon tides build over the next several days.

We flagged this trend last week — said the mackerel schools were thick and the fall striper run was building behind them as water eased toward 60 degrees, and that's exactly what's showing up on the rocks now. Southern Maine's transition season is here. Fish are sliding out of the summer coves and staging around the river mouths and ledges ahead of their run south, and the bait is doing exactly what it does this time of year — pushing hard against structure on the moving tide and dragging predators with it.

Biddeford Pool remains the best hour of striper fishing anywhere on this stretch of coast, and right now that hour is the first two hours of the incoming. Water stacks up against the back channel and the flats off Hills Beach, mackerel get squeezed into the current seam, and bass in the mid-20s to low 30-inch range — with a few better fish pushing 30 pounds reported dockside — are working that seam hard. Big swimming plugs in mackerel patterns, a Bomber Long A or a Yo-Zuri Crystal Minnow worked slow and steady through the current, have been the call. If the fish are up and showing, a topwater like a Gibbs pencil popper worked in short bursts will get eaten too, but don't rush the retrieve — these fish are picking off stunned bait, not chasing.

Pine Point has had the more explosive action of the week. Bluefish have been running the surf line hard on the last two hours of the ebb, chopping through peanut-sized bait pushed out of the marsh systems behind Pine Point and Scarborough. Choppers in the 3-to-6-pound class, with a few bigger fish mixed in, have been hitting metal — a Kastmaster or a Hopkins in the 1.5 to 2-ounce range fished fast — and topwater plugs worked aggressively across the surface. The blitz windows have been short, ten to twenty minutes at a crack, but they've been repeating through the week at the same stage of tide, which tells you the bait is holding a pattern even if the blues are moving around to find it.

Higgins Beach has been more mixed than . There's bait around — small mackerel schools cutting through — but the blitzes there have been spottier than Pine Point's, more a matter of being in the right spot at the right ten minutes than a sure thing. Worth working the outer bar on the incoming with a darter or a Danny-style swimmer if you've got the patience, but don't plan a whole session around it right now.

Prouts Neck has been fishing the way it always fishes best — with a southwest wind pushing bait tight against the rocks on the south side. That wind direction stacks water and forage against structure there, and the stripers know exactly where to sit and wait for it. A bucktail jig tipped with a strip of mackerel belly, worked slow along the bottom in the deeper pockets between the rocks, has been picking up decent fish on the last of the outgoing when the current's still got some push but isn't ripping. Cape Elizabeth's ledges have had a similar bite for anyone willing to work the rocks at low light — smaller fish mostly, but steady enough to be worth the walk.

Flounder action has slowed as expected this time of year — most of that bite has shifted to deeper water and isn't holding shore anglers' attention with the striper and bluefish run building. Cod remain a non-factor from the beach; that's strictly a boat game further offshore and not part of what's happening on this stretch right now.

Looking at the next few days, the bigger Harvest Moon tides should keep sharpening these bite windows rather than blowing them out. Bigger tidal swings mean more water moving through the Pool's back channel and more bait getting pinned against structure at Pine Point and Prouts Neck — that's the mechanism driving all of this, and it should hold as long as the wind stays out of the south or southwest and doesn't turn hard onshore and dirty up the water. If you've only got one morning this week, the smart play is the first two hours of the incoming at Biddeford Pool — that's where the numbers have been most consistent. Keep Pine Point in your back pocket for the last of the ebb if the blues are running, and don't be afraid to check Prouts Neck on any day the wind sits in the southwest quadrant. Expect striper numbers to keep building over the next couple weeks as more of the coastal migration funnels through — this is the start of it, not the peak.
